title: Made to Stick
author: Chip Heath and Dan Heath
blurb: Why do some ideas grab us and refuse to let go, while others vanish the moment we hear them? Chip and Dan Heath argue that sticky ideas are not born lucky. They are built. Studying urban legends, proverbs, ad campaigns and classroom lessons, the brothers find six shared traits. Sticky ideas are simple, unexpected, concrete, credible, emotional, and told as stories. The first letters spell SUCCESs. The main enemy is the Curse of Knowledge. Once we know something, we can no longer imagine not knowing it, so we explain things in abstract, expert language that others cannot grasp. Through vivid examples from business, teaching, medicine and charity, the book shows how anyone can find the core of a message and craft it so people understand it, remember it, and act on it.

lessons.b: Once you know something, you struggle to imagine not knowing it, which is why experts explain things badly and why the Heaths' six principles are needed.
Strip an idea down to its single most important point, the way the military's Commander's Intent tells soldiers what really matters when plans fall apart.
Surprise grabs attention and curiosity gaps hold it, so open a gap in what people know before you fill it.

lessons.t: Concrete: Make It Something You Can Picture
lessons.b: Abstract ideas slip away, while concrete images and examples, like a man on the moon within a decade, give the mind something to hold onto.

scene 6 at 104.9s: text "NO HOOKS" overlaps text "SLIDES OFF"

lessons.b: Ideas become believable through vivid details, human-scale statistics and testable claims that let the audience check the truth for themselves.
People care about one person more than a crowd and about what matters to them personally, so connect your idea to feelings and self-interest.
Stories act like mental flight simulators that move people to act, and they naturally combine all six principles into one memorable message.
